top_choice_rationale: P003 (B016, Persson, Tabellini and Besley) is a mature programme of about three decades that made the policy outcomes of political systems an object of formal analysis and evidence. It explains how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape taxation, spending and public-goods provision. The achievement is broad, has been extended and taught widely, and a citation limited to contemporary rules and fiscal outcomes is distinct from the 2024 prize on the historical origins of institutions. I hold this first place narrowly. Identification of constitutional effects is weaker than in design-based work, and the Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson strands share Persson, so the three-name cut is a judgement. P002 (B001) has the cleanest attribution and is a close second. P001 (B020) has the widest empirical footprint but an unresolved credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum. P004 (B019) has credible designs, but its magnitudes are still debated and the attribution of the task strand is open. An award is better than no award, so P000 is last. The three B016 supporters are not independent assessments, and I give the count no weight.
recusal_note: My profile lists no co-authorship with Persson, Tabellini or Besley. I am a Centennial Professor at LSE and a professor at IIES, Stockholm University. From my own recollection, which my profile does not document and I have not verified, Besley is at LSE and Persson is long associated with IIES, so there is institutional proximity to two B016 candidates. Chair Hassler, a long-term co-author, and Boppart, a frequent co-author, are committee colleagues and not candidates. I am committee secretary, a procedural role with no extra weight. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
